candidates.original_title: Does darkness lead to happiness? Masked suffix priming effects
candidates.description: Masked suffix priming facilitates processing of complex words relative to simple words in adults through overlapping suffixes between prime and target
candidates.citation_sentence: This first experiment replicates the study by Dunabeitia, [20], but with our own stimuli and in child and adult populations.
candidates.notes: The adult results replicate the original Dunabeitia et al. (2008) finding, but fourth and fifth graders show no morphological effect while sixth graders show a marginal effect, yielding a mixed pattern across age groups within one experiment.

candidates.original_title: Does darkness lead to happiness? Masked suffix priming effects
candidates.description: Morphologically complex target words show facilitation when preceded by primes sharing a derivational suffix, whereas simple target words do not show facilitation from merely sharing an orthographic ending.
candidates.citation_sentence: Results in adults replicate previous studies by showing that only the related condition of complex words elicits a significant facilitation (see Dun ˜abeitia, Perea, & Carreiras, 2008).
candidates.notes: The paper reports one experiment with adults and children; the adult outcome is an explicit replication success, while fourth- and fifth-grade children show no effect and sixth graders show only marginal evidence. The entry is coded for the original adult effect, with the added child populations treated as a close extension.
